A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AREAL-DTA and provide readable text, equations, figures, and tables. v1 ends with references; v2 includes additional Appendices A and B. The available material supports comparison throughout.

before.justification: v1 reports original RL reward curves, training throughput, GPU memory measurements, and distributed load-balancing ablations in Section 5.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds sparse-baseline comparisons, GPU-allocation measurements, and low-compression workload results in Section 5 and Appendix B.

M1.justification: The stated chunk scheduling is revised: v1 Section 3.2 describes partial backpropagation followed by continued forward processing, whereas v2 Section 3.2 and Algorithm 3 specify right-to-left backpropagation over completed suffixes. The broader DFS prefix reuse and distributed partitioning design remains; most added pseudocode supplies implementation detail rather than new components.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates tau2-bench workloads. v2 Appendix B.2 adds GSM8K and AIME mathematical-reasoning workloads and a Modified Prefix scenario that removes the common global prompt from tau2-bench and retains leaf sequences, substantially extending coverage to weaker prefix sharing.

E2.justification: v2 Figure 5 adds FlexAttention-based Sparse and Sparse+CKPT comparisons across four model sizes, introducing evaluated prefix-reusing alternatives absent from v1. Existing dense and load-balancing comparators remain. Sparse is described as a proxy for packed-tree approaches, not a direct evaluation of Tree Training.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 and Table 1 change the stated RL algorithm from PPO to GRPO without explaining whether experiments were rerun. v2 also introduces a seven-allocation GPU sweep, low-compression tests with specified checkpointing conditions, compression metrics, and a 24K-token Sparse microbatch budget. The main 16K context and eight-H800 setup remain.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds analyses of rollout/training allocation sensitivity and performance under weak prefix sharing. Existing DFS, block-size, and distributed balancing ablations remain, but v2 no longer separately isolates Cut Tail. Memory analysis contracts from four model sizes in v1 Figure 5 to Qwen3-1.7B in v2 Figure 6.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Both qualitatively acknowledge asynchronous-training nondeterminism without quantifying uncertainty.

E6.justification: v2 adds 1.52–1.70× throughput comparisons against Sparse+CKPT, allocation-sweep results in Table 2, and low-compression results in Table 3. The latter include DTA/AREAL throughput ratios of 0.58 on Modified Prefix and 0.62 on GSM8K for Qwen3-1.7B. The headline 8.31× training and 1.28×/2.28× end-to-end figures remain; the new results do not establish improvements over v1 under unchanged settings.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix B.1 introduces an idealized pipeline-throughput model in Equation 3, and Section 3.2 adds explicit forward/backward operation-count reasoning. The original loss formulation, memory-depth argument, and contiguous-partitioning bound remain, without a new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The DFS and distributed scheduling contributions remain. v2 adds the abstract claim of up to 1.70× throughput over sparse training and narrows v1's broad, consistently favorable performance language to prefix-sharing-heavy workloads. The conclusion also distinguishes the 8.31× training improvement from 2.28× end-to-end throughput.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the blanket quadratic-mask explanation with discussion of packed-tree training states, subtree splitting, and sparse-kernel utilization. Section 5.4 and Appendix B.2 establish a substantive applicability boundary: limited prefix reuse can expose traversal overhead and make DTA slower than dense training. These limitations were largely absent from v1.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link and four algorithms detailing traversal ordering, cache anchors, chunked backpropagation, and partitioning. It specifies default and large chunk sizes of 2048 and 4096, plus Sparse's FlexAttention implementation, 128-token block size, and 24K-token budget. These substantially improve implementation documentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for FlexAttention, DeepSeekMath, GSM8K, and AIME, while removing the PPO reference. Section 2.2 more precisely relates Tree Training to the evaluated Sparse formulation. The broader RL-systems and tree-attention survey remains substantially intact.

P1.justification: The introduction, DFS and chunking explanations, optimization discussion, and evaluation narrative receive substantial rewriting. v2 reorganizes the optimization exposition, adds Section 5.4, and separates detailed algorithms and additional experiments into appendices, materially changing the document's structure and explanation.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, adds a shared-prefix schematic, and relocates the existing DFS illustration to Figure 2. Throughput and load-balancing plots are redesigned with new legends and axis arrangements; memory panels are reduced. New algorithm displays and Tables 2–3 substantially expand the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v1's broad efficiency claims relied on dense comparisons and a high-sharing workload. v2 substantially strengthens their assessment through a relevant sparse comparator, allocation sensitivity evidence, and tests revealing when DTA loses its advantage. Pseudocode and implementation settings also improve reproducibility. Reduced memory-ablation coverage and the unexplained PPO-to-GRPO reporting change are drawbacks, but the comparative evidence and clearer applicability boundaries provide a substantial net improvement.
